title: After 12 years of contracting, AI is bringing the magic back
author: Zenity07
selftext:
I've been trying to find the right words for this post without turning it into a wall of text, so I'll try to keep this short. Edit: of course I failed again, so here's an AI generated TL/DR for you:

>**TL;DR:** After 15+ years of making games, AI finally lets me build my dream game. This video shows the first 10 days, including a map Claude built entirely on its own while I directed it. I'll keep posting updates so you can see whether it holds up as the project grows.

After several decades of making games (about 15 years full time now, with the last 12 years as a contractor), it's only now with AI that I can actually tackle the projects I've always wanted to make. Some people will want to tell me that this is a bad thing, but after decades of trying my best and only seeing the video games industry gradually turn to shit, I'm just all out of fucks to give.

The reason I couldn't do these projects before isn't that I didn't know how to do it, these just aren't the kind of projects you could reasonably do as a solo developer. And even if I had the money to hire an entire team, once the team size and budget grows, it starts to affect the game design and audience you need to target for commercial viability, which means that some ideas simply aren't feasible. That's a big part of the reason why modern games have become so stale, and why it's been increasingly hard for me to find games I actually want to play despite more games being made than ever before.

Last year I was still convinced that AI couldn't reason and would likely never be suitable for game development (at least not the LLM approach). Boy was I wrong. This last year has changed everything, and things have been moving so fast I can't even blame anybody who hasn't quite caught up to it yet. I probably would still not believe it either if I had been too busy to really dive into it myself.

After my last contract I decided to fully commit, started with a few smaller games (I've put some [online](https://wavedash.com/teams/zenity) if you are curious; Rocket Rhythm is a small scoped game I am still working on, the other two are mini web games to test an idea) and now that I am really comfortable with the AI workflow and believe that I have a pretty good idea what can be accomplished with it, I started proper development on my "dream game", the one I've wanted to make for many years (and often tried to start) but never saw a realistic path to getting it done.

So far I've been working on the technical foundations, and most importantly working out an art style and a workflow for building levels, which previously have always been major stumbling blocks for me. The gameplay and characters are still placeholders, but also enough to prove the concept already.

I've asked Claude to make a devlog video illustrating the progress we've made in the first 10 days, and this is the result. The map in the video is entirely made by AI. The workflow for it went something like this:

\* First I developed the art style itself. This actually started by building a custom 3D modelling tool, but when I settled on this style I realized that I don't even need one to create this toy world look from basic building blocks like wooden blocks, cardboard cutouts, and craft sticks.

\* Then I've had Claude clone a few maps and rebuild them using our toolkit to figure out how various layout problems can be solved with it. This also taught us a bunch of lessons for good level design that I've asked it to make a note of.

\* Finally I had Claude build the map based on everything we've learned and iterate on it a few times. I didn't directly touch any part of it, but instead built an in-game editor which lets me mark specific spots on the map and place rulers so I can give the AI targeted instructions for what I want to change.

All assets in the level are procedural, with the exception of the stickers for which I have given Claude an API key for Nano Banana.

The result is not (yet) the best map ever made, but it's certainly a million times better than anything I've been able to do myself before, and exactly what I wanted to start the project with. The speed of development during these first ten days has been out of this world. What's even more insane is that I have worked on a couple more projects on the side during this time.

That said, this is still only a beginning. "Real" game development takes time, and that's still true in the age of AI. What is changing is how ambitious we can be, and I think we'll soon start seeing a lot of experienced solo game developers (and small teams) push themselves further than they ever could without AI.

The common skepticism is that once a project grows large enough, the AI powered workflow starts to fall apart. I don't think so and I haven't seen any evidence for this yet, but the skepticism is fair enough and it's on us to prove it wrong. That's one reason why I want to post early about the development of this game. I hope some of you find this interesting, then I'll make sure to post updates periodically so you can follow along and find out whether it stalls out or not.

In any case, creating another "good enough" game with AI in three days is worthless (unless you are having fun making it, then it's not worthless). I don't believe there are "too many games" yet (where are the games I actually want to play?!), but there are certainly too many \*mediocre\* games and simple clones. Let's aim much higher than that, and I expect that we will see the first real results of that within a few months to a few years from now. That is the future I am really looking forward to both as a developer and a gamer myself.

Now... Whether I will still be able to pay the bills in this future, that's a different question. But as a child I didn't dream of making games to be become rich and famous. So that's a separate concern, and I'm not going to let this stop me from enjoying the ability to actually, finally, make the kind of games six-year-old me dreamed of making almost four decades ago.

On top of that, I find the idea that I just have to accept being made practically redundant as a programmer, but at the same time am supposed to not take advantage of AI myself, absolutely ludicrous. Fuck that.

comments.author: notnotaustin
comments.body: good luck! 240ms is a pretty significant delay though, especially for an fps. do you plan on purchasing us-based server hosting? p2p might be easier for a small project

replies.author: Zenity07
replies.body:
It's a very unique netcode, that's one of the core ideas I've had for a long time that I want to put to a proper test.

240ms normalized latency sounds wild of course, I didn't even think that was possible at first and my original goal was about 150ms) but so far in testing felt perfectly fine. The real test will be with real players of course when the game is more complete, but for now it feels perfectly responsive in my testing with simulated latency.

Matchmaking is always one of the biggest issues for multiplayer games, and even more so for small indie games, so the ability to match people from almost anywhere is a huge deal. There are other benefits too, like actually fair matches (everybody gets exactly the same experience as long as their ping is below 240ms), much less issues with unstable connections, and also somebody who does have a very bad connection can never make your experience worse like it does with other modern netcode implementations.

How it really works would be a longer post though and probably more appropriate for a dedicated video at some point.

State of the art prediction is really good already at hiding most of the delay, I'm just going a step or two further and then also design the gameplay around this fixed delay so it feels significantly better than you would expect. I've experimented with this netcode idea before and I already knew that it works, though for this project Claude has implemented it from scratch based on my description in practically no time which is a big difference to the first time I've had it implement it, where I still had to be extremely explicit and double check every line of code.

replies.author: aGKamui
replies.body:
This is not new netcode wise.

This is literally rollback netcode with a forced ping giga ping? 😭  
  
Latency for FPS is 30ms RECOMMENDED, unsure of what you're even dreaming off trying to pass 200+ as playable.

replies.author: Zenity07
replies.body: Of course I knew most people would and will react like this, but there is more to it. There's no point trying to convince anybody with words that it works well though, the proof will have to be in the pudding.

comments.author: Wonderful_Craft_2332
comments.body: 15 years of making game and this is your dream game?

replies.author: Zenity07
replies.body:
This is for developers interested in the process, I haven't really said anything yet about the gameplay or why it matters to me (and how it doesn't exist yet). I don't expect many here would be the target audience as gamers.

And yes perhaps I should have said \*a\* dream game not \*the\* dream game. It's one I've wanted to make for a long time and the kind of project I would love to work on indefinitely, but that's not the point anyway.
